Exercise 1.1 (Thermal excitation)
In thermal equilibrium at temperature \(T\), the excited and ground states of a qubit with frequency \(f\) are populated in the ratio \(p_1/p_0 = e^{-hf/k_B T}\) (the Boltzmann factor), where \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant. Use \(h/k_B \approx 0.048\) K/GHz.

Compute \(p_1/p_0\) for a 5 GHz qubit at room temperature (300 K), at 1 K and at 10 mK.
Below which temperature is \(p_1/p_0\) smaller than \(10^{-3}\)?
Hint
Take the logarithm of both sides.




Exercise 1.2 (The PRX gate)

Show that \((\cos\varphi\, X + \sin\varphi\, Y)^2 = I\).
Hint
Expand the square, and use that \(X\) and \(Y\) anticommute.

Write \(\gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi)\) as a \(2\times 2\) matrix.
Hint
Use Equation 1.1, which applies because of (a).

Check that \(\gate{PRX}(\theta,0) = R_X(\theta)\) and \(\gate{PRX}(\theta,\pi/2) = R_Y(\theta)\). Which rotation is \(\gate{PRX}(\theta,\pi)\)?



Exercise 1.3 (Turning one Pauli into another)
Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be Pauli strings that anticommute, \(PQ = -QP\).

Show that \(e^{-i\alpha P/2}\, Q\, e^{i\alpha P/2} = \cos\alpha\, Q - i\sin\alpha\, PQ\).
Hint
Write both exponentials with Equation 1.1, and use \(PQP = -Q\).

Show that \(R_Y(\pi/2)\) turns \(Z\) into \(X\), and that \(R_X(-\pi/2)\) turns \(Z\) into \(Y\).
Hint
Use (a), and the products of Pauli matrices.

Check that the circuit of Figure 1.8 implements \(e^{-i\theta\, Z\otimes Y\otimes X/2}\).
Hint
Use Equation 1.5, the identity for CZ in the text, and (b).

Draw a circuit of CZ gates and \(R_X\) or \(R_Y\) rotations for \(R_{ZZ}(\theta)\), and compare it with Figure 1.6.
Hint
Start from \(R_X(\theta)\) on the second qubit, conjugate it by CZ, then turn the remaining \(X\) into \(Z\).




Exercise 1.4 (Virtual Z gates)

Show that \(R_Z(\alpha)\, X\, R_Z(\alpha)^\dagger = \cos\alpha\, X + \sin\alpha\, Y\) and \(R_Z(\alpha)\, Y\, R_Z(\alpha)^\dagger = \cos\alpha\, Y - \sin\alpha\, X\).
Hint
Use Exercise 1.3 (a) with \(P = Z\).

Write the Hadamard gate, up to a global phase, as a single \(\gate{PRX}\) pulse followed by a \(Z\) rotation.
Hint
Write the Hadamard gate as \(R_Z(\alpha)\,R_Y(\beta)\,R_Z(\gamma)\) first, then use Equation 1.7.




Exercise 1.5 (The cost of distance)

Check Figure 1.11 on the four computational basis states.
We want to implement a CNOT between the qubits at opposite ends of a line of \(n\) qubits, using SWAPs. If the qubits may stay in their new positions after the operation, how many CNOTs are needed? And if they must be returned to their original positions?
Hint
Each SWAP moves a state one step along the line.

If the qubits must be returned to their original positions, can you implement the same CNOT with fewer CNOTs, without SWAPs?
Hint
Start with \(n = 3\), and follow what each CNOT does to the bits of a basis state \(\ket{abc}\).




Exercise 1.6 (SWAP from native gates)
On a device whose native gates are \(\gate{PRX}\) and CZ, a SWAP must be built from these.

Let \(A\) be a single-qubit unitary. Show that \((I\otimes A)\,\gate{CZ}\,(I\otimes A^\dagger)\) applies \(AZA^\dagger\) to the second qubit if the first is in \(\ket{1}\), and does nothing if it is in \(\ket{0}\).
Hint
Write \(\gate{CZ} = \ket{0}\bra{0}\otimes I + \ket{1}\bra{1}\otimes Z\).

Find a \(\gate{PRX}\) rotation \(A\) with \(AZA^\dagger = X\), and write a CNOT as one CZ and two \(\gate{PRX}\) gates.
Hint
Exercise 1.3 (b) gives a suitable \(A\).

Using Figure 1.11, write a SWAP with three CZs and \(\gate{PRX}\) gates only. How many \(\gate{PRX}\) pulses does it need?



Exercise 1.7 (A shot budget)

How many shots give a standard error of 0.01 when \(\langle P\rangle \approx 0.9\)? Compare with \(\langle P\rangle \approx 0\).
Hint
Solve Equation 1.9 for \(N\).

You need ten expectation values, each from its own circuit, each with a standard error of at most 0.005. Assume the worst case, \(\langle P\rangle = 0\), and assume that loading each circuit takes 10 s, with no queue. Estimate the total time on a superconducting device and on an ion trap. Which part of the time dominates on each?
Hint
Use the times per shot of Table 1.5.




Exercise 1.8 (An error budget)
A device has the native gates \(\gate{PRX}\) and CZ, with virtual \(Z\) rotations. Its operations fail independently, with probability \(10^{-4}\) for a \(\gate{PRX}\) pulse, \(5\times10^{-3}\) for a CZ and \(10^{-2}\) for a measurement. On a line of 10 qubits, numbered 0 to 9, we run a brick-wall circuit: each layer applies \(R_Z\) and \(R_X\) to every qubit, followed by CZs between neighbouring qubits, on the pairs (0,1), (2,3), … in the first layer and every second layer after it, and on the pairs (1,2), (3,4), … in the other layers. Figure 1.12 shows two layers on four qubits. The circuit has 8 layers and ends by measuring all qubits.



Two layers of a brick-wall circuit on four qubits.



Count the native operations of each kind, and estimate the probability that a run of the circuit has no error at all. Which kind of operation contributes most to the failures?
Hint
Which gates in Figure 1.12 need a pulse?

How does the answer to (a) change on a device without virtual \(Z\) rotations, where each \(R_Z\) needs a pulse with the same error as \(\gate{PRX}\)?
Roughly how many layers can the circuit have before the probability of a run without error drops below one half?
Hint
\((1-p)^n \approx e^{-np}\) for small \(p\).




Exercise 1.9 (Readout errors bias the estimate)
Suppose that the readout of each qubit reports the wrong bit with probability \(p\), independently in every shot and for both outcomes.

Show that the recorded sign \(s\) of a single-qubit \(Z\) measurement has expectation value \((1-2p)\langle Z\rangle\).
For a Pauli string \(P\) acting on \(k\) qubits, show that the recorded sign has expectation value \((1-2p)^k\langle P\rangle\).
Hint
The recorded sign is the true sign times one independent factor \(\pm 1\) per qubit.

Take \(p = 0.02\), \(k = 4\) and \(\langle P\rangle = 0.5\). Compare the bias of \(\bar s\) with its standard error for \(N = 10^3\) and for \(N = 10^5\) shots. When do more shots stop helping?
Hint
The standard error is given by Equation 1.9.

If \(p\) is known, how can the estimate be corrected? What does the correction do to the standard error?



Exercise 1.10 (Measuring in other bases)
A device has the native gates \(\gate{PRX}\) and CZ, and measures in the computational basis.

Which \(\gate{PRX}\) pulses must be applied before the measurement to estimate \(\langle X\otimes Y\otimes Z\rangle\)?
Hint
On each qubit, you need a rotation \(U\) with \(U P_j U^\dagger = Z\); see Exercise 1.3.

Can \(\langle X\otimes I\rangle\) and \(\langle X\otimes X\rangle\) be estimated from the same shots? And \(\langle X\otimes X\rangle\) and \(\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle\), if only single-qubit rotations are allowed before the measurement?

title: Appendix A — Exercises
section: Chapter 2: Noise channels and error budgets
text:
Chapter 2: Noise channels and error budgets

Exercise 2.1 (Random phases)
A qubit undergoes the rotation \(R_Z(\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is a Gaussian random angle with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\).

Show that \(\mathbb{E}[\cos\theta] = e^{-\sigma^2/2}\).
Hint
\(\cos\theta\) is the real part of \(e^{i\theta}\).

Which dephasing probability \(p\) does this channel have? What is it for \(\sigma \ll 1\)?



Exercise 2.2 (Composing depolarising channels)

Apply the depolarising channel with parameter \(p_1\) and then the one with \(p_2\), using Equation 2.5. Show that the result is again a depolarising channel, and check that its factor is \((1-p_1)(1-p_2)\).
A qubit is prepared in \(\ket{+}\), and \(n\) noisy \(X\) gates are applied, each followed by depolarising noise with parameter \(p\). What is \(\langle X\rangle\) at the end? For \(p = 10^{-3}\), after how many gates has \(\langle X\rangle\) fallen to half of its initial value?
Hint
Where in the circuit can the channels be moved?

Two qubits each undergo depolarising noise with parameter \(p\), independently, so that the channel on both is \(\Lambda\otimes\Lambda\). By which factors do \(\langle Z\otimes I\rangle\) and \(\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle\) shrink? Do these factors depend on the state of the two qubits?
Hint
A product of channels acts factor by factor: \((\Lambda\otimes\Lambda)(A\otimes B) = \Lambda(A)\otimes\Lambda(B)\).




Exercise 2.3 (Relaxation and dephasing together)

Show that amplitude damping and dephasing commute. Write the Bloch vector of \(\ket{+}\) after it has been idle for a time \(t\).
Hint
Compare what the two channels do to \(\rho_{00}\), \(\rho_{11}\) and \(\rho_{01}\).

Suppose the calibration data of a superconducting device give, for three of its qubits, \(T_1 = 150\), \(80\) and \(200\) µs and \(T_2^* = 120\), \(150\) and \(60\) µs. Compute \(T_\varphi\) for each qubit. Which process limits the coherence of each, relaxation or dephasing?



Exercise 2.4 (The echo)

Show that \(X R_Z(\theta) X = R_Z(-\theta)\), and that \(R_Z(\theta/2)\, X\, R_Z(\theta/2) = X\) for every angle \(\theta\). An echo on an idle qubit ends with a second \(X\). Why does this second \(X\) cost nothing extra when the next gate on the qubit is a single-qubit gate?
Hint
Use \(XZX = -Z\) and Equation 1.5. For the second \(X\), see Section 1.3.5.

In a Ramsey experiment, the qubit frequency is shifted by an amount \(\delta\) that is constant within each shot, and Gaussian with standard deviation \(\sigma_\delta\) across shots. Ignoring relaxation and fast noise, show that the coherence after a wait \(t\) is \(e^{-\sigma_\delta^2 t^2/2}\). What is it with an echo?
Hint
Use Exercise 2.1 with \(\theta = \delta t\).




Exercise 2.5 (Coherent and incoherent errors)

A gate has a coherent over-rotation of \(\eta = 0.01\). After how many repetitions is the error probability 1%? Answer the same question for random over- and under-rotations, with mean zero and standard deviation \(\sigma = 0.01\).
An \(R_X(\theta)\) gate has a small coherent error: it applies \(R_Z(\eta)\) after the intended rotation. For each repetition of the gate, independently and with probability \(1/2\), we add a perfect \(X\) gate just before it and another just after it. Since \(X\) commutes with \(R_X(\theta)\), the ideal gate is unchanged, but the error becomes \(X R_Z(\eta) X\). Show that, averaged over these random choices, the error of each gate becomes a dephasing channel with \(p = \sin^2(\eta/2)\). How does it now add up over \(n\) repetitions?
Hint
Use Exercise 2.4 (a), and compute the factors.




Exercise 2.6 (Unequal readout errors)
A qubit has the readout error rates \(e_0 = 1\%\) and \(e_1 = 4\%\).

Which value of \(\langle Z\rangle\) is recorded on average for the states \(\ket{0}\), \(\ket{1}\) and \(\ket{+}\)?
Suppose instead that the readout is perfect, but that preparing \(\ket{0}\) gives \(\ket{1}\) with probability \(e_p\), and that \(\ket{1}\) is prepared by a perfect \(X\) gate after that. Which confusion matrix does an experiment that prepares \(\ket{0}\) and \(\ket{1}\) and measures them report? Can it tell this situation apart from a readout error?
Why does the difference between the two situations matter for a circuit with gates between the preparation and the measurement?
Hint
Where in the circuit does each error act, and what do the gates do to it?




Exercise 2.7 (The largest visible circuit)
Take the brick-wall circuit of Table 2.2 with \(L\) layers instead of 8, and suppose that the ideal value of \(\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle\) is \(0.5\). We take \(10^4\) shots and call the signal visible if the measured value is at least three standard errors away from zero.

Write the signal left, \(f\), as a function of \(L\) for each platform.
Hint
Split the contributions of Table 2.2 into a part per layer and a fixed part.

What is the largest \(L\) with a visible signal on each platform? How long do the gates of the \(10^4\) shots take in total on the ion trap?
Which contribution limits \(L\) on each platform? Which improvement would help the ion trap most?



Exercise 2.8 (When more shots stop helping)

Show that \(N^* \approx (1 - \langle P\rangle^2)/\big(\langle P\rangle^2 (\sum_i\varepsilon_i)^2\big)\) when the total error \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) of the circuit is small.
For the superconducting brick-wall circuit of Table 2.2 with \(L\) layers and \(\langle P\rangle = 0.5\), compute the exact \(N^*\) for \(L = 1\), 8 and 30. Why are more shots worth taking on a better device?
Exercise 1.9 (c) compared \(10^3\) and \(10^5\) shots. Compute \(N^*\) there, and explain the result of that comparison.



Exercise 2.9 (GHZ states under local and global noise)
The GHZ state \((\ket{0\cdots 0} + \ket{1\cdots 1})/\sqrt{2}\) on \(n\) qubits has \(\langle X\otimes\cdots\otimes X\rangle = 1\), with \(X\) on all qubits, and \(\langle Z\otimes Z\otimes I\otimes\cdots\otimes I\rangle = 1\), with \(Z\) on the first two qubits only.

Each qubit undergoes depolarising noise with parameter \(p\). By which factors do the two expectation values shrink?
Which parameter of the global depolarising channel shrinks \(\langle X\otimes\cdots\otimes X\rangle\) by the same factor? What does it then do to \(\langle Z\otimes Z\otimes I\otimes\cdots\otimes I\rangle\)?
How could measurements of these two expectation values show whether the noise on a GHZ state is closer to local or to global depolarising?



Exercise 2.10 (Dephasing from an environment)
A qubit in the state \(\alpha\ket{0} + \beta\ket{1}\) interacts with an environment qubit in the state \(\cos(\phi/2)\ket{0} + \sin(\phi/2)\ket{1}\) through a CZ gate, after which the environment is discarded.

Show that the qubit undergoes a dephasing channel with \(p = \sin^2(\phi/2)\).
Hint
With the environment second, \(\gate{CZ} = I\otimes\ket{0}\bra{0} + Z\otimes\ket{1}\bra{1}\). Take the partial trace over the environment.

The Kraus operators of this channel are \(K_e = (I\otimes\bra{e})\,\gate{CZ}\,(I\otimes\ket{E})\) for \(e = 0, 1\), where \(\ket{E}\) is the initial state of the environment. Compute them, and compare them with those of Definition 2.3.

title: Appendix A — Exercises
text:
Chapter 3: Measuring and simulating Hamiltonians

Exercise 3.1 (Pauli decompositions)

Write \(M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1-i \\ 1+i & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) as a sum of Pauli matrices.
Write the SWAP gate as a sum of two-qubit Pauli strings, and conclude that \(X\otimes X + Y\otimes Y + Z\otimes Z = 2\,\gate{SWAP} - I\). Which eigenvalues does a bond term of the Heisenberg model have, and for which states?
Hint
Use Equation 3.3, and compute each trace as a sum over the basis states \(\ket{ab}\).

Show that \(e^{-i\theta\,\gate{SWAP}} = \cos\theta\, I - i\sin\theta\,\gate{SWAP}\). What does this gate do to \(\ket{10}\)?
Hint
Check which property of \(P\) the derivation of Equation 1.1 used.




Exercise 3.2 (The TFIM on two qubits)
The TFIM on two qubits is \(H = -JZ_1Z_2 - h(X_1 + X_2)\).

Write \(H\) as a \(4\times 4\) matrix in the basis \(\ket{00}, \ket{01}, \ket{10}, \ket{11}\).
Show that \(H\) maps the states \(\ket{00}+\ket{11}\) and \(\ket{01}+\ket{10}\) into combinations of each other, and the states \(\ket{00}-\ket{11}\) and \(\ket{01}-\ket{10}\) to multiples of themselves. Find the four eigenvalues, and show that the ground-state energy is \(-\sqrt{J^2 + 4h^2}\).
What are the ground states for \(h = 0\) and for \(J = 0\)? Is the ground state entangled for \(J = h\)?



Exercise 3.3 (Measurement settings)
How many measurement settings does \(H = Z_1Z_2 + Z_2Z_3 + X_1 + X_2 + X_3 + Z_1X_2\) need, with single-qubit rotations only? Give the settings and the terms that each measures.
Hint
Look for terms that cannot pairwise share a setting.



Exercise 3.4 (Shots for groups)
A Hamiltonian is measured in several settings, with single-shot variances \(\sigma_g^2\).

Show that the best split of \(N\) shots gives setting \(g\) a number of shots proportional to \(\sigma_g\), and that \(N = (\sum_g \sigma_g)^2/\varepsilon^2\) shots give the standard error \(\varepsilon\).
For the TFIM chain with \(n = 10\), \(J = 1\) and \(h = 0.2\), assume that the terms of each group are uncorrelated and \(\sigma_i = 1\). How many shots go to each setting for a standard error of 0.1? How many would an equal split need?
A study reports the energy of a state of this chain with a standard error of 0.1 from 200 shots in total. Is the claim plausible? What would have to be true of the state?



Exercise 3.5 (The commutator of the TFIM)
Take the TFIM chain of Definition 3.3, with \(A\) the bond terms and \(B\) the field terms.

Show that \([Z_1Z_2, X_1] = 2i\,Y_1Z_2\), and that \(Z_iZ_{i+1}\) commutes with \(X_j\) for \(j \ne i, i+1\).
Show that \(\|[A,B]\| \le 4Jh(n-1)\).
Hint
Write \([A,B]\) as a sum of Pauli strings, and bound its norm by its Pauli 1-norm.




Exercise 3.6 (The cost of a step on a device)

How many CZs does one Trotter step of the TFIM on an \(L\times L\) square lattice cost on a device with a square coupling graph?
Place a \(3\times 3\) lattice on a line of 9 qubits, along a path like that of Figure 3.2 (c). Which bonds join qubits that are not neighbours on the line, and how far apart are they?
Implement each such bond by moving one of its qubits next to the other with SWAPs, applying \(R_{ZZ}\), and moving it back. Without cancelling any gates, how many CZs does one step cost now?
Hint
A SWAP is three CNOTs (Figure 1.11), and each CNOT is one CZ with single-qubit gates (Exercise 1.6).




Exercise 3.7 (How many steps?)
A circuit evolves a system for a time \(t = 1\), with \(a = 1\) in Equation 3.11, on a device with \(\varepsilon_{\text{step}} = 0.01\).

Compute \(r^*\) and the two terms of the infidelity at \(r^*\). How do they compare? Is this a coincidence?
The device improves tenfold, to \(\varepsilon_{\text{step}} = 0.001\). By which factors do \(r^*\) and the smallest infidelity change?
Back at \(\varepsilon_{\text{step}} = 0.01\), suppose we use a bound that overestimates \(a\) ninefold, as in the example of the text. How many steps do we choose, and what is the infidelity of the circuit, with the true \(a = 1\)?



Exercise 3.8 (Light cones and classical simulation)

In the Trotter circuit of Figure 3.4 on a long chain, on which qubits of the initial state can \(\langle Z_i\rangle\) depend after \(k\) steps?
On a square lattice, each step has four layers of bond gates, two along the rows and two along the columns. Which qubits can \(\langle Z_i\rangle\) depend on after \(k\) steps, and how many are they?
A laptop can simulate about 30 qubits exactly. For how many steps can it compute \(\langle Z_i\rangle\) exactly on a chain of 1000 qubits, and on a square lattice of 1000 qubits?



Exercise 3.9 (The energy of a noisy state)
A circuit prepares a state of the TFIM chain of \(n\) qubits, but each qubit undergoes local depolarising noise with parameter \(p\) (Definition 2.7) just before the measurement. Write \(E_A\) and \(E_B\) for the ideal expectation values of the bond terms and of the field terms.

Which energy does the measurement give on average, in terms of \(E_A\), \(E_B\) and \(p\)?
For \(n = 10\), \(p = 1\%\), \(E_A = -6\) and \(E_B = -5\), compute the bias. Compare it with the standard error of 0.1 of Section 3.4.1. Do more shots help?
If \(p\) is known, can the bias be removed by dividing the estimate by a single factor, as in Section 2.7.2? How else?

title: Appendix B — Glossary
text:
1/f noise

Noise in which slow fluctuations are much stronger than fast ones, in inverse proportion to their frequency. It typically comes from many defects, each switching at its own rate.

amplitude damping

The channel that describes relaxation: a qubit in the excited state decays to the ground state with probability gamma, which grows with time as one minus exp(-t/T1).

average gate fidelity

The state fidelity between the output of a noisy gate and the ideal output, averaged over all pure input states. One minus it is the error per gate.

bias

The difference between the average of an estimator and the true value. Noise biases estimates of expectation values; more shots do not reduce the bias.

bit flip

The Pauli channel that applies X with some probability p: it flips the bit of a qubit. Readout errors with equal error rates act as a bit flip just before the measurement.

Bloch vector

The three expectation values of X, Y and Z of a qubit, which fix its density matrix. It has length one for pure states and less for mixed states.

brick-wall circuit

A circuit whose two-qubit gates act on alternating pairs of neighbouring qubits, first (1,2), (3,4), and so on, then (2,3), (4,5), and so on, like the bricks of a wall.

calibration

Measuring and adjusting the control pulses of a device so that its gates do what they should. Providers publish calibration data: the error rates of each qubit and gate at the last calibration.

coherence

The off-diagonal entry of a qubit’s density matrix, which carries the relative phase of a superposition. Its size decays over the dephasing time T2*, or over the longer time T2 with an echo.

coherence time

How long a qubit keeps its quantum state, in particular a superposition, before noise from its surroundings destroys it.

coherent error

A systematic error in which a gate applies the wrong unitary, for example a rotation by a slightly wrong angle, in the same way every time.

completely positive

A map of density matrices is completely positive if it still gives valid density matrices when it acts on part of a larger system. Quantum channels are exactly the completely positive maps that preserve the trace.

confusion matrix

The table of probabilities of reading each outcome given each true state of the qubits. It describes readout errors.

correlated errors

Errors that affect several qubits together, or that depend on what happens elsewhere in the circuit, such as crosstalk or bursts caused by cosmic rays.

correlation function

An expectation value of a product of observables on two qubits, such as Z on qubit i times Z on qubit j, which shows how much the two qubits agree and how this changes with their distance.

coupler

A circuit element between two superconducting qubits through which they interact. A tunable coupler can switch the interaction on and off.

coupling graph

Graph whose vertices are qubits and whose edges are the pairs on which a native two-qubit gate is available.

cross-resonance

A two-qubit gate mechanism for superconducting qubits with fixed couplings: one qubit is driven at the frequency of its neighbour.

crosstalk

An unwanted effect of an operation on one qubit on other qubits, for example through couplings that are never fully switched off.

density matrix

The general description of a quantum state, including states that are uncertain mixtures of pure states: a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one. Expectation values are traces of the observable times the density matrix.

dephasing

Loss of the relative phase of a superposition without loss of energy, for example because the qubit frequency is shifted by an unknown amount. The measured times T2* and T2 include both dephasing and relaxation; the time of pure dephasing alone is called Tφ.

dephasing channel

The Pauli channel that applies Z with some probability p, also called the phase-flip channel. It keeps the probabilities of 0 and 1 and shrinks the coherence. An unknown phase, for example from an unknown shift of the qubit frequency, acts as a dephasing channel.

depolarising channel

On one qubit, the Pauli channel that applies X, Y or Z, each with probability p/4. It is the same as replacing the state by the maximally mixed state with probability p, and it shrinks the Bloch ball uniformly. On many qubits, it can be local or global.

depth

The number of layers of gates in a circuit that must run one after another. Gates on different qubits can share a layer.

digital quantum computer

A quantum computer that runs circuits: sequences of gates from a fixed universal set, applied to qubits and followed by measurements. Also called gate-based, as opposed to analog devices that imitate the time evolution of a physical system directly.

dilution refrigerator

A refrigerator that reaches about 10 millikelvin, cold enough that heat no longer excites superconducting qubits.

dispersive readout

Readout of a superconducting qubit through a resonator whose frequency depends slightly on the qubit state. A weak microwave probe tells the two states apart.

DiVincenzo criteria

A checklist for building a quantum computer: scalable, well-characterised qubits; preparation of a known state; long coherence; a universal set of gates; measurement of individual qubits.

dynamical decoupling

Repeated echo pulses during a long wait, which remove noise that is slow compared with the spacing of the pulses. It suppresses noise on the device itself.

echo

An X pulse halfway through a wait, which reverses the phase accumulated before it, so that phase errors that stay constant during the wait cancel. An echo experiment measures T2.

error mitigation

Methods that reduce the effect of noise on estimated quantities without correcting the errors, typically by running extra or modified circuits and combining their results. They cost extra shots.

estimator

A rule that turns measured data into an estimate of a quantity, for example the sample mean of the outcomes as an estimate of an expectation value.

fidelity

A number between 0 and 1 measuring how close a state or operation is to the intended one. The state fidelity is the probability that a state passes a test for the target state; the average gate fidelity averages it over all input states. Informally, one minus the probability of an error.

Floquet circuit

A circuit that repeats the same layer of gates many times, like a system driven periodically in time. With large Trotter steps, it follows the exact evolution under a Hamiltonian that differs from the intended one.

geometrically local Hamiltonian

A Hamiltonian on qubits placed on a chain or lattice, whose terms each act only on qubits within a fixed distance of each other, for example single qubits and pairs of neighbours. Every qubit appears in only a few terms, so the number of terms is proportional to the number of qubits. A stronger property than k-locality.

global depolarising channel

The depolarising channel acting on all qubits at once: with probability p, the state of all qubits is replaced by the maximally mixed state. It shrinks every Pauli expectation value by the same factor, whatever its weight.

ground state

The eigenvector of a Hamiltonian with the lowest eigenvalue, the state of lowest energy. A system that is cold enough settles in or near its ground state.

Hamiltonian

The observable of the energy of a system, a Hermitian matrix. Its eigenvalues are the possible energies, and it also determines how the state of the system changes in time.

Heisenberg model

A spin model with the coupling XX + YY + ZZ on every pair of neighbouring qubits. Each bond treats the three axes alike, and the number of qubits in the state 1 is conserved.

incoherent error

A random error that differs from shot to shot and averages to a noisy channel. Random errors accumulate more slowly than coherent ones.

ion

An atom with one or more electrons removed, so that it carries an electric charge and can be held by electric fields.

ion trap

A device that holds ions in vacuum with electric fields, typically lined up in a chain a few micrometres apart.

Josephson junction

A thin insulating barrier between two superconductors. In a circuit it makes the energy levels unevenly spaced, which is what turns the circuit into a usable qubit.

k-local Hamiltonian

A Hamiltonian that is a sum of terms that each act on at most k qubits, with k fixed as the number of qubits grows. As a sum of Pauli strings, it has polynomially many terms instead of exponentially many. Often simply called a local Hamiltonian.

Kraus operators

A set of matrices that defines a quantum channel: the channel maps a density matrix to the sum of each Kraus operator times the density matrix times its adjoint. The same channel can have different sets of Kraus operators.

laser cooling

Slowing the motion of atoms or ions with laser light until they are almost at rest.

leakage

An error in which a qubit leaves its two qubit levels, for example when a transmon is pushed into its third level.

light cone

The qubits that an operation, an error or a change can influence after a given number of circuit layers or a given time. In a circuit of nearest-neighbour gates, it grows by a fixed number of qubits per layer; a local Hamiltonian also spreads changes at a finite speed.

local depolarising noise

Depolarising noise that acts on each qubit separately and independently. It shrinks the expectation value of a Pauli string by one factor for each qubit on which the string acts, so strings of higher weight shrink faster.

locality

The principle that physical interactions involve only a few particles at a time, usually ones close to each other in space. It is why the Hamiltonians of physical systems are local, with polynomially many terms instead of exponentially many.

logical qubit

A qubit of information encoded in many physical qubits by an error-correcting code. Its error rate can be much lower than that of the physical qubits.

magnetisation

The average over the qubits of the expectation value of Z: the average alignment of the spins along z.

Markovian noise

Noise without memory: the noise after each operation does not depend on what happened before. The model in which every gate is followed by a fixed channel assumes it.

mean squared error

The average of the squared difference between an estimate and the true value. It equals the bias squared plus the variance.

measurement setting

A choice of basis (X, Y or Z) for every qubit, made with single-qubit rotations before the measurement. Each shot of a setting gives a value of every Pauli string whose factors agree with it.

mixed state

A quantum state that is not pure: a probabilistic mixture of pure states, described by a density matrix. On one qubit, its Bloch vector lies inside the Bloch sphere.

Mølmer-Sørensen gate

The standard two-qubit gate of trapped ions. Laser beams couple two ions to the shared vibrations of the chain, producing an entangling rotation of any chosen angle.

native gate

A gate the hardware implements directly with a calibrated control pulse. Every other gate must be compiled into native gates.

NISQ

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum: devices with tens to thousands of qubits whose errors are not corrected, so noise limits the size of the circuits they can run.

noise model

A description of the noise of a device, gate by gate and qubit by qubit, used to simulate noisy circuits, for example built from the calibration data of the device.

operator norm

The largest factor by which a matrix can stretch the length of a vector. For a Hermitian matrix, it is the largest absolute value of its eigenvalues.

optical tweezers

Tightly focused laser beams that hold single neutral atoms in place and can move them.

Pauli 1-norm

The sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of an operator written as a sum of Pauli strings, often written lambda in the literature. It sets the worst-case number of shots needed to estimate the energy, and it bounds the operator norm.

Pauli channel

A channel that applies a random Pauli error, chosen with fixed probabilities. It multiplies the expectation value of each Pauli string by its own factor.

Pauli string

A tensor product of single-qubit Pauli matrices (I, X, Y or Z), one for each qubit, such as ZZ or XIY. Hermitian, and squares to the identity.

phase-flip channel

Another name for the dephasing channel, the Pauli channel that applies Z with some probability p. The name describes its Kraus form; physically, dephasing is usually a gradual loss of information about the phase.

phonon

A quantum of vibration. In an ion trap, phonons are the quanta of the vibrations that the whole chain of ions shares; in a solid, such as a qubit chip, they are the quanta of the vibrations of the crystal.

phonon bus

The shared vibrations of a chain of trapped ions, used as a common channel through which any two ions can interact in a two-qubit gate.

physical qubit

A qubit as implemented in hardware, for example one transmon or one ion, with all its imperfections.

pulse

A short burst of microwave or laser radiation at a chosen frequency, switched on and off smoothly, used to drive a qubit. Its frequency selects which qubit responds; its area and phase set the rotation.

pure dephasing

The part of dephasing that does not come from relaxation, described by a dephasing channel whose strength grows with time, with characteristic time Tφ. It cannot be measured on its own, since relaxation also reduces the coherence.

purity

The trace of the square of a density matrix: 1 for pure states, smaller for mixed states, and smallest, one over 2 to the n, for the maximally mixed state of n qubits (1/2 for a uniformly random qubit).

QCCD

Quantum charge-coupled device: a trapped-ion architecture in which ions are moved between zones of the trap, so that any two ions can be brought together for a gate.

quantum advantage

A task that a quantum computer solves better than any classical method, faster, more cheaply or more accurately. For a task of a given size, it is a claim against the best classical methods known, and it is lost if better ones are found.

quantum channel

The general description of how a quantum state changes, including noise: a linear map of density matrices that can be written with Kraus operators. Unitary gates are the channels with a single Kraus operator.

quantum dot

A tiny region in a semiconductor that can trap single electrons.

quantum error correction

Encoding quantum information redundantly in many physical qubits, so that errors can be detected and corrected without disturbing the encoded information.

qubit-wise commuting

Two Pauli strings are qubit-wise commuting if, on every qubit, their factors are equal or one of them is the identity. Such strings can be measured from the same shots, in one measurement setting.

Ramsey experiment

A measurement of dephasing: a pulse puts the qubit in a superposition, the qubit waits, and a second pulse turns the remaining coherence into a measurable population. It measures T2*.

random telegraph noise

Noise from a defect that switches at random between two states, making the qubit frequency jump back and forth.

randomised benchmarking

A method to measure the average error per gate: random gate sequences of growing length, which ideally return to the initial state, are run, and the decay of the success probability with the length gives the error per gate.

relaxation

Loss of energy by a qubit: the excited state decays to the ground state. Its characteristic time is called T1, and the amplitude-damping channel describes it.

resonance

Radiation drives a transition between two energy levels only when its frequency matches their energy difference divided by Planck’s constant. This is how individual qubits are addressed.

Rydberg state

A state of an atom in which one electron is excited very far from the nucleus. Atoms in Rydberg states interact strongly over micrometre distances.

Schrödinger equation

The equation that relates states to the Hamiltonian. In its time-independent form, it is the eigenvalue equation of the Hamiltonian; in its time-dependent form, it says how a state evolves, and its solution applies the unitary exp(-iHt).

scrambling

A property of circuits, such as deep circuits of random gates, that spread every error over all the qubits, so that any error leaves the output close to random. For such circuits, global depolarising noise is a good model of local noise.

shot

One run of a circuit: prepare the qubits, apply the gates, measure. Returns one bit string.

SPAM errors

State preparation and measurement errors, characterised together because a measurement right after a preparation cannot tell them apart.

spin

An intrinsic two-level property of an electron (spin-1/2: up or down), which can serve as a qubit.

state fidelity

For a pure target state, the probability that a state passes a test for the target, that is, the expectation value of the projector onto the target.

SWAP

A two-qubit gate that exchanges the states of two qubits. It costs three CNOTs.

T2*

The dephasing time: the time over which the coherence of a qubit decays in a Ramsey experiment. It is shorter than T2, measured with an echo, because it also includes slow noise that the echo removes.

tensor network

A classical description of a quantum state as a network of small arrays, one per qubit, whose size grows with the entanglement. Efficient for weakly entangled states, such as those of a chain evolved for a short time.

threshold

The physical error rate per operation below which error correction helps: below it, larger codes give lower logical error rates.

transmon

The most common superconducting qubit: a small circuit with a Josephson junction, whose two lowest energy levels form the qubit.

transpilation

Compilation of a circuit into the native gates and coupling graph of a device, including inserting SWAPs and simplifying.

transverse-field Ising model

A spin model with a ZZ coupling on every pair of neighbouring qubits, which favours aligned neighbours, and a field along x on every qubit, which favours the state plus. Abbreviated TFIM.

Trotter formula

An approximation of the evolution under a sum of terms by a product of evolutions under each group of terms in turn, repeated in many short Trotter steps. Its error, the Trotter error, comes from terms that do not commute and decreases as the number of steps grows.

twirling

Inserting random Pauli gates around a gate, chosen so that they cancel in the ideal circuit. Averaged over the random choices, any error becomes a Pauli channel.

unital

A channel is unital if it maps the maximally mixed state to itself; on one qubit, it keeps the centre of the Bloch ball fixed. Pauli channels are unital; relaxation, described by amplitude damping, is not.

virtual Z gate

A Z rotation implemented by shifting the phase of all later drive pulses instead of applying a pulse. It takes no time and adds no error.

weight

The number of qubits on which a Pauli string acts with a Pauli matrix other than the identity. Under local noise, strings of higher weight lose their expectation value faster.
